name: Brownish
lede: Brownish is a hedge word turned into a color: a reddish mid-brown from Ridgway's 1912 color standards, named for a thing that is nearly, but not quite, brown.

sections.title: A word that means almost brown
sections.body:
Brownish is a qualifier, not a color with a history of its own. Paterson's dictionary defines it with a single line, listing it as one of the *-ish* words, and that is all it says [1]. The suffix hedges: a thing is not quite [[brown]], or it is brown with something else in it.

Naturalists and mineral collectors leaned on this hedge. Werner's Nomenclature of Colours, the 1814 Edinburgh edition by Patrick Syme, lists Brownish-red and Brownish-black among its named shades, and Baty shows earlier mineral descriptions built the same way [2]. Ridgway, the American ornithologist, gave Brownish its own plate in 1912, and our swatch is his, plate XXVIII [3]. The ISCC-NBS system later filed it under light reddish brown, about 6.4 units away from our swatch [3].

sections.title: What the books mean by it
sections.body:
In the color books the word nearly always flags a hue that was altered by something, such as age, a mixture or dirt. Pastoureau notes that before the mid-fourteenth century most black cloth was not really black but looked grayish, bluish or sometimes brownish [4]. Ball describes a Venetian painting whose radiant azurite sky had become a muddy brownish-mauve before its cleaning in 1967-8 [5]. The dark foliage and brownish landscape of Pollaiuolo's *Apollo and Daphne* are the discolored remains of green copper resinate, not the painter's intention [5]. And Gage notes that the brownish spots on the pale grass in a Seurat canvas come from the darkening of zinc yellow [6].

It can also be praise. In 1557 Dolce admired the brownish softness of flesh tints that he credited to Apelles [6]. Gurney, describing early paints, calls the dug-out iron oxides, the earths from which Siena took its name, brownish reds and oranges [7]. A fashion color once had a related name: *caca-dauphin*, a brownish yellow, was all the rage in the last weeks of 1751 after the birth of Louis XV's first grandson [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 971 carry a color within six CIEDE2000 units of this swatch over at least five per cent of the canvas, which is 4.1 per cent [8]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so many of these are the browning the books describe, not the painter's first color [8].

It peaks in the 1100s to 1500s, with a rate 2 to 3 times the archive's, and then drops in the 1600s [8]. Indian works carry it 5.2 times as often as the archive (154 of 721), and Pontormo has it in 5 of 13 works [8]. The painting with the most of it is Thomas Eakins' *The Chaperone*, at 65 per cent of the canvas, and the oldest is a funerary papyrus [8]. In printed English the adjective peaks in the 1920s [9].

questions.answer: A hue that has been altered, by age, mixing or dirt

questions.q: Why do the dark foliage and landscape in Pollaiuolo's Apollo and Daphne look brownish?

openers: A brownish sky in an old painting is often a blue that has aged, not the painter's first choice.
Brownish was a standard word in nineteenth-century color lists for describing rocks and birds.

issues: Short article by design: the books treat brownish as a descriptive word; no name history beyond Ridgway 1912 and Werner/Syme.
Baty p.32 shows Werner's lists; mineralogist flint example is from the same page (Lenz).
Ball plate captions cited by chapter 11; the cleaned Venetian picture is not named in our excerpt.
Caca-dauphin: Pastoureau gives late 1751 and the birth of Louis XV's first grandson.
